newsitem.title: UK: Dutch seek bulk cocoa delivery to LIFFE contracts.
newsitem.headline: Dutch seek bulk cocoa delivery to LIFFE contracts.

text.p: The Dutch cocoa trade seeks changes in the London futures contract to allow delivery of bulk cocoa, fast becoming the norm in shipments to the Netherlands.
Louis Bensdorp, president of the Dutch Cocoa Association (NCV), said he would meet officials of the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) on the subject on Wednesday.
Using bulk shipment, beans are taken out of their bags at the port of origin for quality checks then all subsequent transport and storage is carried out in bulk, for a considerable saving on costs.
Use of containers is another option, although savings are less.

Bensdorp said he would discuss with LIFFE ways in which present specifications permitting delivery of cocoa only in its original jute bag could be adjusted. As an interim compromise, cocoa could be rebagged in importing countries, he said.
"I would expect them to allow re-bagging just for the time being," Bensdorp told reporters on Tuesday after a presentation to the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO).
The NCV is also in talks with the Cocoa Association of London and its French counterpart, AFCC, to design a new bulk cocoa contract.

Importers in the Netherlands, the hub of European processing, pioneered bulk shipments from the Ivory Coast last year. Dutch traders now receive up to 10,000-tonne shipments and are considering larger tonnages for maximum cost effectiveness.
Total bulk shipments were expected to reach 250,000 tonnes in 1996/97 rising to 300,000 in 1997/98 and some 80 percent of all Dutch cocoa processing in the next few years, Bensdorp said.
"It will become necessary in London to allow bulk cocoa," he added.

He also said that a squeeze in the London futures market last year that sent prices to eight year highs of 1,172 stg per tonne as a trader took delivery of 300,000 tonnes of cocoa, could have been avoided if bulk cocoa was deliverable at the time.
"A lot of cocoa which could help to ease the squeeze could not be used," Bensdorp said.
A LIFFE official said bulk shipments were under review but a decision to amend specifications rested with the Board.
In his presentation to ICCO members, Bensdorp said bulk shipments had the advantage of faster loading, discharging and storage without impairing quality.
But there were still problems that needed to be overcome, he said.

Dependance on weather conditions was one disadvantage. Weather needed to be completely dry for loading and unloading and in countries like Britain where rain was common, this could lead to severe port delays.
In tropical origins, the quality of cocoa could be affected if ships' hatches don't close in time to protect the beans from sudden downpours.
There are also worries on the part of the producers, who face additional costs of structural changes that are required for bulk shipments but no financial benefit.
"It's about time that some of these savings find their way to the exporter countries," said Sam Appah, representative from Ghana.
Kouame N'Guessan of Ivory Coast's Caistab called for logistical support from importing countries saying their handling costs had increased.
But Bensdorp said producers should work out ways in which they could trim their costs.
"We believe in free enterprise. If there is a possibility of exporting bulk at lower cost, exporters will find a way to do so," he said.
